title: Super El Niño set to peak in December, with impacts expected well into 2027
content: The ongoing super El Niño could become the strongest on record since 1950, with the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) forecasting a peak around December 2026. Sea surface temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region of the equatorial Pacific have reached record levels, with anomalies projected to rise to approximately 3.7°C above normal. Around 2.6 billion people worldwide could experience unusually high temperatures through December, according to meteorologist Ben Noll. Drought conditions could intensify across parts of India, Africa, Central and South America, Indonesia and the Pacific, while extreme rainfall could threaten around 1.3 billion people globally. The WMO forecasts a near-100% likelihood of El Niño persisting through February 2027, with its influence on weather patterns potentially continuing into spring. The ongoing El Niño event in the equatorial Pacific Ocean, which is already breaking records, is projected to become the strongest since observations began in 1950, potentially surpassing even the 1876-1878 El Niño, whose strength is known only from reconstructed data. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) forecasts that the event will peak around December, but a super El Niño has already developed. The possibility of a super El Niño has been discussed by weather agencies and climate scientists for several months, and their forecasts are now materialising. Sea surface temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region, an area of the equatorial Pacific Ocean used to measure the strength of El Niño, have already reached unprecedented levels. “This year's El Niño continues its climb into uncharted waters; Niño3.4 region anomalies are now at a 3.4°C above normal (how fitting!), higher than any prior El Niño event on record,” wrote Zeke Hausfather, a climate scientist at Berkeley Earth and a lead author of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's Seventh Assessment Report, on social media platform X (formerly Twitter). “September monthly Niño3.4 anomalies also set a record at 2.9°C (beating 2015 and 1877's 2.75°C),” he added. “This El Niño became the strongest one on record during September and is headed for a near 4°C peak in December,” wrote Ben Noll, a meteorologist with the Washington Post, on X. “That will have major — and in some cases unprecedented — effects on weather patterns. Impacts will vary by region,” he added.

title: Winged guests are coming early to Chilika, and they are telling us something
content: Reports from Chilika this week say its winged migratory guests have already begun arriving in the first weeks of October. The Odisha Forest Department has intensified patrolling, 22 temporary bird-protection camps are in operation, and northern pintails, Eurasian wigeons, gadwalls, shovelers, glossy ibises and several other species are already being spotted around the lake and Nalabana. For many newspapers, this is a feel-good winter story. For anyone who has watched Chilika for three or four decades, however, it is also an ecological signal worth watching carefully. We must be cautious here. October arrival is not entirely new. Historical reports show migratory birds reaching Chilika in the second half of October, and sometimes even earlier. So I would not describe this year’s October arrival, by itself, as an unprecedented shift of two or three weeks. What is changing, however, is the variability of the migration calendar — and the climatic conditions into which these birds are arriving and from which they eventually depart. That deserves our attention. The Chilika Wildlife Division broadly describes the migratory season as lasting from October to March. Numbers generally build through winter, with large congregations during November, December and January, while many birds begin their return journey from March onwards. But the climate at both ends of this journey is changing. So is the journey itself. In February 2021, reports from Chilika and neighbouring Bhitarkanika noted that migratory birds had begun leaving earlier than usual. Rising temperatures and declining water levels were cited among the factors. Maximum temperatures in Bhubaneswar during February had also been unusually high in the preceding years. This is consistent with a larger climatic trend. Studies of Odisha’s temperature record show a clear warming tendency. Research covering 1981-2010 found about 0.3°C warming over three decades, with a particularly sharp rise in surface temperatures during 2001-2010. More recent analyses of the 1980-2020 period also show predominantly positive temperature trends across Odisha. India, too, has warmed substantially. The India Meteorological Department estimates a long-term warming trend of about 0.62°C per century in annual mean temperature during 1901-2020. These numbers may appear small. But ecological systems do not experience climate change as a single annual average. A shift of even a fraction of a degree can alter the timing of flowering, insect emergence, fish breeding, water availability and, for migratory birds, the availability of food along an entire flyway. The climatic character of Chilika’s winter is changing. It is becoming warmer and more unpredictable. That matters to birds that have evolved around seasonal cues. Chilika’s winter visitors do not simply decide one morning to fly south. Many come from the vast Central Asian and Palaearctic region, including Siberia and areas around the Caspian and Arctic regions. Their migration is shaped by a complex combination of temperature, snow, ice, food availability, daylight, water conditions and ecological cues along the flyway. Those cues are changing rapidly. The Arctic is warming much faster than the global average. Earlier snowmelt and changing spring conditions are altering the ecological calendars of Arctic-breeding birds. Recent research published in Nature Climate Change , examining GPS and body-mass data from several Arctic-breeding waterfowl populations, found that some birds are advancing their spring migration by reducing the time they spend refuelling and by travelling faster. In other words, birds are not merely responding to a warmer world by changing where they go. They are changing when and how they travel. This does not mean we can say climate change alone caused this year’s early arrival at Chilika. Migration is far too complex for such a simple conclusion. Conditions at breeding grounds, staging areas, food availability, winds, temperature and wetlands along the flyway all matter. But it does mean that early arrival deserves to be viewed as one signal within a much larger climate-driven ecological transformation. The birds are caught between two changing worlds: an increasingly warmer north and a warming wintering ground in the south. A migratory bird does not need Chilika merely to be beautiful. It needs Chilika to function. It needs adequate water, suitable salinity, aquatic vegetation, fish and invertebrates, mudflats, roosting grounds and relatively predictable seasonal conditions. If these ecological conditions change, the consequences can extend far beyond the birds. We already know that changes in Chilika’s hydrology affect its fish, aquatic food web and water quality. A decline in fish populations, for example, is not simply a livelihood problem for fisherfolk. It can disturb predator-prey relationships and destabilise the wider lake ecosystem. This is why counting birds once a year is not enough. We need to understand what the birds are telling us about the lake itself. Here is where I believe conservation is making a fundamental mistake. We count birds. We count fish. We count tourists. But we rarely count the knowledge of the people who have lived with Chilika for generations. During my recent interactions with traditional fisherfolk from places such as Arakhakuda, Satapada and Mahisa along the Magarmukh channel, I was reminded again of how much ecological intelligence exists outside our formal monitoring systems. They can read the lake in ways no mobile application can fully reproduce. They know when the pani begins changing from sweet to saline, when the wind shifts from uttara to dakshina , how tides alter fishing conditions, when fish begin appearing in particular stretches and how the character of the water changes with the season. They remember when the birds arrive. They remember where they used to congregate. They notice when particular fish breed earlier or disappear. They notice changes in fog, wind, rainfall, water depth and salinity. This is not merely folklore. It is local ecological knowledge — a living climate record built over generations. We should institutionalise it. Imagine a community-based Chilika climate and biodiversity monitoring system in which fisher youth and women are trained as para-ecologists. Their observations of water levels, salinity, temperature, wind, fish breeding, first bird arrivals and unusual ecological events could be recorded alongside satellite observations, India Meteorological Department data and scientific surveys. That would give us something extremely valuable: a living early-warning system for the lake. Protecting Chilika is not merely about preventing poaching or removing plastic. It is about protecting the ecological processes that make Chilika a living wetland. That means maintaining healthy freshwater flows from its catchments, protecting its connections with the sea, keeping its channels and mouths functioning naturally, monitoring salinity and water quality, regulating ecologically damaging aquaculture and other pressures, and ensuring that fisher communities have both a stake and a voice in the management of the lake. A healthy Chilika is not created by protecting birds from people. It is created by protecting the ecosystem on which both birds and people depend. This is where climate change makes the challenge more complicated. The lake is not an isolated ecosystem. It is connected to rivers, the sea, catchments, agriculture, aquaculture, settlements, fisheries and the atmosphere. Climate change therefore becomes a water story, a biodiversity story and a livelihood story at the same time. So, should we celebrate the arrival of the winged guests? Of course. But perhaps we should also pause. An early or unusually timed arrival should not become just another photograph for the annual winter tourism calendar. It should trigger a question: what has changed along the flyway, and what is changing inside Chilika? The answer will not come from one bird count, one satellite image or one temperature reading. It will come from putting together the memories of fisherfolk, the observations of birdwatchers, the measurements of scientists, satellite data and long-term climate records. The birds are not climate scientists. But they are remarkably sensitive ecological indicators. They respond to changes that we may notice only much later. That is why we should listen carefully when they arrive. Because the warning may not be that the birds are coming early. The warning may be that the seasons on which both birds and people have depended for generations are becoming less predictable. If we fail to understand that change, we may eventually have a Chilika that is still beautiful, still famous and still full of birds in photographs — but no longer capable of supporting the ecological abundance that made it famous in the first place. The winged guests are here. Let us not merely count them. Let us listen to what they are telling us.

title: Wayanad is losing its cool: India’s closely watched Western Ghats hill district is getting warmer
content: For years, Wayanad in Kerala has been watching its weather more closely than perhaps any other hill district in India. The Hume Centre for Ecology and Wildlife Biology, based in district headquarters Kalpetta, has built a community weather-monitoring network across the district, measuring rainfall and temperature at hundreds of locations. What began after the devastating floods and landslides of 2018 and 2019 has grown into one of India’s most extensive local weather-monitoring experiments. Since 2024, Hume has collected rainfall data from more than 200 locations, using rain gauges and thermometers maintained with community participation. The network has since expanded, offering an unusually detailed picture of local weather patterns. And what the instruments are recording is worrying. Wayanad, bordering the Nilgiris in Tamil Nadu and Kodagu in Karnataka, is warming. The change is unsettling a hill district long known for rain, mist, cool nights and green mountains. Its climate shaped everything from coffee and pepper cultivation to tourism and everyday life. Now, this sought-after hill destination is gradually losing some of the climatic charm that made it special. The latest measurements from the Hume Weather Lab provide a striking snapshot. Between September 1 and 17, 2026, the average temperature in Wayanad was 29.2°C, compared with 27.3°C in 2023, 27.2°C in 2024 and 27.3°C in 2025. This was about 1.9°C above the average for the previous three years. Maximum temperatures remained above 30°C for seven consecutive days, from September 11 to 17, touching 30.7°C on September 15. The highest temperature recorded so far this year was 34.4°C on April 18. Exposed soil temperatures touched 39°C during the first 17 days of September, with readings above 30°C on several days. Rainfall was limited to four isolated events, while the average minimum temperature was 20.9°C. The significance lies not simply in a few hot days, but in the combination of heat, soil temperature, moisture stress and uncertain rainfall. For a landscape whose agriculture, forests and settlements evolved around a relatively cool, wet climate, the consequences could be profound. Wayanad forms part of the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve and the larger Western Ghats ecosystem. Its mountains, forests and valleys sustain numerous streams. The Kabini, one of Kerala’s major east-flowing rivers, originates in the region before flowing into Karnataka and joining the Cauvery river system. The monsoon has shaped the district’s agricultural rhythms. Heavy rain replenished streams and paddy fields, while forests retained moisture and moderated local temperatures. Coffee, pepper, arecanut and other crops developed around a particular sequence of rainfall, sunshine and cool nights. Tourism grew around the same climatic advantage. Visitors from Kerala’s hotter plains travelled to Wayanad for misty mornings, pleasant afternoons and cold evenings. Resorts, plantation stays and wildlife tourism were marketed as an escape from the heat. That promise is becoming less certain.

title: Daily weather tracker: Weather takes a turn; snowfall in higher Himalayas, heavy rain alerts across several states
content: Summary Heavy rainfall alerts issued for southern states as Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka brace for thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds. Fresh snowfall across higher Himalayan regions intensifies cold conditions, while Uttarakhand faces heavy rainfall warnings and possible disruptions to highway connectivity. Delhi-NCR to experience dry weather with partly cloudy skies as temperatures hover around 34 degrees Celsius following monsoon withdrawal. Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh brace for rainfall, possible snowfall and thunderstorms, prompting caution for mountain travellers. Southwest monsoon withdrawal continues across India, while above-normal temperatures persist in several regions despite changing weather patterns and rainfall warnings.
